content: Typhus fevers are a group of infectious diseases caused by specific types of bacteria that are transmitted to humans through vectors such as fleas, lice, and chiggers. These diseases include murine typhus, epidemic typhus, and scrub typhus, each associated with a distinct bacterial species and mode of transmission. The most common clinical manifestations of typhus fevers are fever, headaches, and, in some cases, a rash. Murine typhus, also referred to as flea-borne typhus, is caused by the bacterium Rickettsia typhi. This disease is primarily transmitted to humans through contact with infected fleas, particularly the Oriental rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) and the cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis). Epidemic typhus, also known as louse-borne typhus, is a rare disease caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii. It is spread to humans through contact with infected body lice. Scrub typhus, sometimes called bush typhus, is caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. This disease is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected chiggers, which are the larval stage of mites.
